JoH.tiTowR,June 4.^Four days have^elapsed since the angel of death swept^through the valley of Conemaugh, but no^ray of sunshine has yet lightened the scene^of horror at Johnstown bridge. The sky^is still overcast with heavy clouds and the^sun rests behind the heavy pall as though^reluctant to view, the handiwork of his^tent elements. For thirty-six hours^Ore engines played upon the smoking ruins^above the bridge, but the flames would^break out afresh at intervals and seem to^defy the subduing force of the water.^Nearly two thousand men are employed in^different parts of the valley tearing up^ruins and prosecuting the search for the^undiscovered dead.

I'he investigations are not without fruit^^ful results, for the bodies of the charred^victims of the flood and fire are discovered^with undiminished frequency. It becomes^more and more apparent that not a single^vestige will ever be recognized of the hun^^dreds roasted in the flames above the^bridge, since the last sentence was penned^a party of searchers unearthed a charred^and unsightly mass from the smouldering^debris within thirty yards of ti e Asso^^ciated Press headquarters. It required the^authoritative verdict of physicians to dem^^onstrate that the ghastly discovery was the^charred remains of a human being. Only^the trunk remained, roasted beyond all^semblance to flesh. Five minutes work re^^vealed fragments of a skull, that at once^disintegrated of its own weight when ex^posed to the air, no single piece being^larger than a half dollar, and the whole re^^sembling remnants of shattered charcoal.

Withinan hour and a half a dozen dis^^coveries in ways more or less horrifying^were made by the searchers as they raked^with picks and hooks in the smoking rains.^So difficult is it at times to determine^whether the remains are human beings^that it is apparent that hundreds must be^fairly burned to ashes. Thus the number^that have found a last resting place be^neat these ruins can at best never be more^than approximated.
Moxham,the iron manufacturer, mayor^pro tem of Johnstown, to-day is probably

thebusiest man in the United States. Al^^though for days without sleep, he sticks^nobly to his task. Hundreds of others are^like him, and men fall only from sheer^fatigue. There are many who have not^closed an eye in sleep since they awoke^Friday morning. They are hollow-eyed^and pitiful-looking. Many lost near rela^^tives and friends. Some of the unfortun^^ates who could not go to the different trains^endeavored to ^^ attaint flour from wrecked^stores in Johnstown. One dealer was^charging S5 a sack for flour. Suddenly the^crowd heard of the occurrence, and several^desperate men went to the store and de^^livered flour gratuitously to the homeless^aaa stricken people. Another is selling^flour at 51.50 a sack. He refused to give^any away, guarding his store with a shot^^gun.

Thebodies recovered in Johnstown to^^day have been robbed by ghouls that flock^to the scene. It is known that one lady^had several hundred dollars in her posses^^sion just after the disaster, but when the^body was recovered not a cent was in her^pocket.
TheHuns attacked the supply wagon be^^tween Morrillville and Cambria City to^^day. The drivers repulsed them, but they^again returned. A second tight ensued,^but after lively scrambling the Huns were^again driven away. After that the drivers^and guards of supply wagons were permit^^ted to go armed.

Registersare being opened in Johns^^town, and all the survivors are requested^to register in order to give information of^their safety to inquiring friends.
Hourby hour the calamity grows. Every^moment now the body of some new victim^is taken from the debris and the town is^^ne vast charnel house. The scenes at the^extemporized morgue are bey ond descrip^^tion in ghastliness, while the moans and^groans of the suffering survivors, tossing^in agony with bruised and mangled bodies^or raving in a delirium of fever in the nu^^merous temporary hospitals, make even^the stoutest hearted quail with terror.^Nearly 2,000 bodies have already been re^covered, and as the work of examining^progresses the conviction grows that the^magnitude of the calamity has not yet^been approximated.

Conservativesestimates this morning put^the number of lost at 7,000 and many men^of calm judgment not wont to exaggerate,^who have been upon the ground from the^outset, place the number at 10.000.
Thefirst relief train bearing thousands of^pounds of provisions for the suffering and^twi thousand coffins for the dead, passed^over the Johnstown bridge across an im^^provised trestle|to the Johnstown depot this^morning. For the first time railroad com^^munication has been re-established be^^tween the stricken city and the outside^world.
Inthe early morning hours, and up to 9^o'clock, ISO bodies had been taken from^the ruins. Most of them are unrecogniza^^ble, and they are being taken away and^buried as fast as possible. In a vast num^^ber of cases the bodies are almost com^^pletely burned, but the clothing or some^^thing of the kind frequently makes the^Identity complete. What is needed now^more than anything else are gravediggers.^This morning hundreds of bodies were^lying around and there was no one to dig^graves. At least fifty funerals have^already passed the Associated Press^headquarters. It is not an unusual^thing to see two or three coffins^carried along, one after another, and fol^^lowed by a number of mourners, all in the^same family. It is Impossible to obtain^conveyances of any kind: consequently all^the funeral possessions are on foot Gen.^Hastings has ordered the Fourteenth regi-^medt to Johnstown to relieve the sher.ffs,^who are worn oat. He is hiring all the^men he can to remove the debris. The^Pittsburg contractors have a number of^men at work, and have a placard calling^for 2,000 men. The Cambria Iron works^are already preparing to get their works in^operation, and will probably have two fur^^naces in operation at the end of the week.

Itis not believed now that the fire in the^wreck at the bridge can be extinguished^for weeks. The hand of providence is in^It. The suggestion made by physicians yes^terday that bodies not burned be allowed^to be cremated in the interest of public^health, which aroused such a storm of in^^dignation among surviving friends, is^viewed with more calmness to-day. There^is a growing sentiment that it is after all^the best solution of the problem. Weeks,^and probably months, will be required to^remove the stupendous mass by artificial^means, and in the meantime the putrefy^^ing remains of humanity buried therein^will be doling out polution and death to^ail the surrounding country.

Johnstown,June 4.^It is now definit -^ly settled that at least twenty to forty pe ^.^pie were lost on the two sections ^ f the dry^express that left Pittsburg Friday morn^^ing and on the Johnstown accommodation^about to leave Johnstown that afternoon.^There have been numerous conflicting re^^ports about how many trains were caugl.t^m the flood, but from the most reliab.'e^sources it has been ascertained that thn e^trains were caught by the water. A pas^^senger on one train says he can count cp^at least twenty whom he saw drown.

WilliamHenry smith, of the Associated^Press, gives the following account of seen- s^on one of the trains caught in the flood:^The number of passengers on the day ex^^press known to have been lost is six. Bo-^sides these there are two ladies missing and^unaccounted for, but who may yet be alive.^The conductor who was at Conemaugh on^the fateful day claims to have have run^through the cars and told the passengers to^run to the mountains. The passengers who^survived are anxious to make the ac^^quaintance of that conductor. They cer^^tainly neither saw him nor heard him. His^intention may have been good, but the^good deed was omitted. When the passen^^gers reached the mountain side they found^there two conductors in beautiful white^caps. Their manner was calm and their^clothing unspotted. 1 asked one of them^why he did not notify the passengers of the^breaking of the dam. He replied.^In some confusion that he^had no time. His companion^made a report to his superior, which re^^port was carried over the mountain by a^passenger that night, but there was noth^^ing in it to indicate that any of the passen^^gers were any of his concern. He reported^the loss of two trains, in striking contrast^to the neglect of duty of these conductors^It is pleasant to note the manly conduct of^others. The first^always the first men^^tioned^should be the locomotive engineer^and fireman, whose bravery and devotion^were conspicuous. They never neglected^to give such warning as they could in the^face of danger, in some cases of certain^death. A brakeman riding deadhead,^whose name can not be recalled, rendered^splendid service in rescuing the vsuen^and children at the risk of his own life. s.^Aleer, the Piniman conductor was efficient^and cool headed. H. E Wooddyer, cook^of the ear Aragon. and John H. Waugh.^porter of the parlor ear, C. H. Loris. stood^manfully by G. F. Giffrith*. of the Norwich^line, in the rescue of passengers. It was^Wooddyer who stood on the top of the car^Aragon with axe in hand ready to cut the^roof to prevent the smothering of those^within. We think better of our race with^such examples before us.

A Monster Water Wave Sweeys Down the

The Breaking of a Great Dam Across the

One of the Most Horrible Calamities of

New Florence, Pa., Junel. - One
hundred bodies have been recovered at
Nineveh.
Seventy persons are reported bnrned to
death in the fire at Johnstown bridge.

W. M. Hays has just returned from
Johnstown and says the place is annihi
lated. Conemangh is wrecked and Cambria
City is swept away. Fully 1,200 lives are
lost.
Pittsburg, Jnne 1. - Persons returning
from the scene of the disaster say at least
three thousand people have lost their lives.
It is stated at the office of the
Pennsylvania railroad early this morning that
the deaths would run up into thousands.
The stream of bnman beings swept
before the angry floods was something
most pitiful to behold. Men, women and
children were carried along, frantically
shrieking for help, but resene was
impossible. Husbands were swept past their
wives, and children were borne aloDg'at a
terrible speed to certain death before the
eyes of their frantic parents. It is said at
the depot it is impossible to estimate the
number of lives lost. It will simply be a

matter of conjecture for several days as to
who were lost or who escaped.
New Florence, Pa., June 1. - Sang
Hollow is the nearest point to Johnstown
that can be reached this morning. It is
impossible to secure definite information,
but there seems to be no donbt that
Johnstown was inundated and fnlly one
thousand lives lost.
Jnne 1. - At 1:30 this

Philadelphia, Jnne 1. - At 1:30 this
morning news received from Bolivar stated
that two-story honses, barns, stables,
whole forests of trees, onthonses, smoke
honses, railroad bridges, connty bridges,
rafts, inverted skiffs and driftwood by the
acre were floating by, from all of which
imploring hands were stretched ont to those
on the banks, willing but impotent to
help. At Lockport, two miles east, twenty

New Florence, Pa., June 1 - The gray
morning light does not seem to show either
hope or mitigation of the awful fears of the
night. The Associated Press
correspondent drove across the mountains to New
Florence, fourteen miles from the
scene of devastation at Johnstown.

The weary, overworked newspaper man,
who has been without rest and food since
yesterday afternoon, and the telegraphers
who bandied his messages are even now
preparing for the work of the day. Even
here, so far from the washed oat towns,
horror is in oar midst. Seven bodies have
been fonnd on the shore near this town, two
in a tree, a man and woman, where the
tide carried them. The country people are
coming in in large numbers, telling stories
of disaster along the river banks in
seqne8tered places.

John McCarthy, who lives in Johnstown,
reached here at 4 o'clock. He left
Johnstown at 4:30 yesterday. He says the scene
is indescribable. The people had been
warned early in the morning to move to
the highlands, bnt did not heed the
warning, although repeated a number of times,
np to one o'clock, when the
oncoming water poured into the streets
several feet deep. Then honses began
rocking to and fro, ond finally the force of the
current carried buildings across the streets
and vacant lots and da-r ed them against
each other, breaking them into fragments.

These buildings were freighted with poor
wretches who shortly before laughed at
the cry of danger.
McCarthy says in some places he
counted fifteen persons clinging to
buildings. It is impossible to get to Johnstown
proper to-day in any manner except by
row-boat. The only hope is to get within
three miles of Johnstown by special train
or by hand-car. This will be done by the
Associated Press agent within the next
ho.ur.
New Florence, Pa., June 1 - The
waters are now receding here as rapidly as
they rose last night, and as the banks are
nncovered the dead are showing np.
Already nine dead bodies, five of them
women, have been picked np within the
limits of this borough since daylight. None
are jet recognized. One beantifnl woman,
25 years old, bad clasped in her arms a
babe six months old.

Tbe dead body of a yonng man was
discovered in tbe branches of a hnge tree
which had b- eu carried down stream.
All orchard ciopsand shrubbery along the
banks of the river are destroyed.
Tbe body of another woman has just
been discovered in the river here. Her
foot was discovered above the surface of
the water. A rope was fastened about it
and tied to a tree waiting assistarce to
land.
Webber and wife, an old coQDle, Mike
Metzgar and John Forney were rescued near
here this morning. They bad been carried
from their home in Cambria City on the
roof of a bouse. Several others were on
the roof of the house when carried off and
all were drowned. They were unknown to

Webber, they having drifted on to the roof
from floating debris. Webber and wife
were thoroughly,! drenched and almost
helpless from exposure and were nnahle to
walk when taken from the roof.
New Florence, Pa., Junel. - There has
grown up a bitter feeling among the
surviving sufferers against those who owned
the lake and dam and damage suits will be
plentiful. It is impossible to tell what
the loss will be, bnt at nine o'clock the
coroner of Westmoreland connty sent a
message, saying a hundred bodies had
been recovered at Nineveh. Sober minded
people do not hesitate to say 1200 is a
moderate estimate of the drowned.

"How can anybody tell how many are

"I have been at Sang Hollow since 11

J. W. Esch, a brave railroad employe,
saved sixteen lives at Ninevah.
The most awfnl calumniation of the
awful night was the roasting of a hnndred
or more persons in Milford by fire. The
rnins of houses and outbuilding and other
strnctnres swept against the new railroad
bridge at Johnstown, and from an
overtnrned stove or some other cause the npper
part of the wreckage caught fire. There
were crowds of men, women and children
on the wreck. Their screams soon added
to the awfnl chorus of horror. They were
literally roasted in the flood. Soon after
the fire had burned clear out other houses

were thrown against the mass, and there
were fifty people in sight when the rnins

bridge into pitchy darkness.
The latest news from Johnstown is that
bnt one or two houses could be seen in,the
town. It is also said that but three.hoases
remain in Cambria City.

Pittsburg, Jnne 1. - Bodies from the
scene of the disaster are beginning, to
arrive here.
New Florence, Pa., Jane 1. - The
banks on both sides of the river are
crowded with anxious watchers, and with
horrifying frequency their vigils are
rewarded by the discovery of dead bodies.
Within the last half hoar three floating
bodies have been recovered at this point.
Hundreds of people from Johnstown and
np-river towns are harrying here in search

night's flood, and the most intense excite
ment prevails. The street corners are
crowded with pale, anxious people, who

Bodies are being prepared for burial, bat

Four boys have just come from the river
bank above here. They say that on the
opposite side a number of bodies can be
seen lying in tbe mod. They found the
body of a woman on this side.
R. B. Rogers, justice of the peace at

that 100 dead bodies have been ionnd at

From this one can estimate that the
loss of life will reach over 1,000 and

gness, the sickening sight that is expected
to be met by correspondents when they
arrive at the scene.

Report is j net received that twenty
persons were on an island near Ninevah and
a man and woman are seen on a partly
submerged tree. Another report says at
least one hundred people were consnmed
in the flames at Johnstown last night. It
is said to have been an awful horror.
Tbe air is filled with thrilling and almost
incredible stories, bnt none of them as yet
are confirmed. It is certain, however, that
the worst cannot be imagined.
Pittsburg, Jnne 1. - The body of an

Sang Hollow, Pa., Jnne 1. - Fathers
pressed their faces against the car windows
in the vain endeavor to see something,
they knew not what. They knew in a
measure of the dreadful fate their loved
ones had met with All along the raging
Conemangh the train stopped and bodies
were takeD on the express car that were
being carried by servivors out along 'he
banks.
What a journey was that of the last half
hoar! Swollen, awful corpses lay here and
there in piles of cross ties or on the river
banks among taDgled greenery. About 9
o'clock the first passenger train since
Friday reached New Florence with a load of
eager passengers. Staring out of the
windows, with red eyes among them, were

tongh lookirg Hungarians and Italians
who had lost friends near Nineveh, while

the passengers on tbe tiain were a man and
wife from Johnstown. A little womam
said : "Onr's is a big new bnckhonse. It
is a three-story honse, and I don't think
there is any trouble; do yon ? There are my
fonr children in the house and their nurse,
and I gness father and mother will go over
to the honse, don't yoo ?"
In a few moments all those in the car
knew tbe story of the pair, and many
a pitying glance was cast at them. Their
house was one of the first to go.

STATE RELIEF FUND.
Governor Beaver to Devote $1,000,000
for Restoration Purposes in
Conemaugh Valley.
IN COUNCIL.
Governor Heaver Fledges the
Necessary Relief Fund.
JOHNSTOWN, Pa.. June 9. - An
important meeting was held here this afternoon,
at which Governor Beaver, Adjutant
General Hastings and others were present. A
i-eueral discussion of the situation was had.
Chairman McCreery, of the relief
committee. said he though* it was time the relief
committee was relieved of the work of
clearing away the debris by the State
The Governor said all the necessary money
could be raised; that there were 200 men who
would become responsible for $5 000 each;
that he would give his bond to the State
Treasurer for $1,000,000, with those 200
men as bondsmen, and the State Treasurer
would then pay out $1,000,000 for the
necessary work. W hen the legislature

met the money withdrawn from the
treasury could be appropriated. He said the
money already subscrilied should be used
entirely for the relief of the sufferers,
and the money from the State Treasury
should lie used for restoring the vicinity to its
condition before the Hood. All debts already
contracted for the removal of the debris
paid out for this purpose from
the relief fund, should be refunded, so that
every cent subscribed for the rekel of the
stricken people shall be used for that
parpose alone. The Governor has $250,000 in
his hands now for the rebel fund. A
committee of seven well-known men of the
State will be appointed to distribute the
relief fund, and the present relief
committee is to continue until the commission is
appointed. In an interview to-night Gov.

Beaver said: ''The funds which have come
into my hands from so many quarters
outside of the State, and which have been
imposed upon me as a sacred trust, will be
expended wholly and absolutely lor the
benetit of individual sufferers. No part of
it will be expended in the work, which is
legitimately the domain of the State under
its police powers.
Health Bulletin.
Johnstown, June 9. - The following
bulletin has been issued by the State Board
of Health and speaks for itself. It is
posted to-day in every conspicuous place.

The bulletin reads :
Health Bulletin: - The general condition
of health in Johnstown and vicinity is
excellent. No epidemic disease of any kind
prevails, nor is it expected any will arise.
The mill region has been divided into
districts and each placed under a ^tnnpetent
sanitarian. The Ittate Board of Health is
prepared to meet all emergencies as they
arise. The air is wholesome and the water
generally pure If the good people of the
devastated district will go on as they have
so nobly done for the past week in their
efforts to clean up the wreckage good
health will certainly be maintained.

(Signed) George G. Groff.
What Dr. boll Says.
Johnstown, Jnue 9. - Dr. Goff says that
the valley has been swept so clean by the
great floods that the rivtr waters are purer
than ever before the disaster. There is a
difference in the contaminating power of
the decomposing organic matters that come
from the bodies of the dead of contagious
diseases, that would be tar more dangerous
than those bodies Irom the river which are
generally covered with from one to six feet
of mud and sand. This earthy matter
absorbs all the effluvia and acts as the
best of disinfectants. There is no present
danger to the water supply of Pittsburg
and Johnstown. The only present danger
is from the people being frightened into
sickness by sensational reports.

Coroner's Verdict.
Greensburg, Pa., June 9. - The coroner
of this county has returned inquisitions on
the bodies of 218 victims of the Johnstown
flood. The verdict in each case is that
deceased came to his death by violence due
to the flood caused by the breaking of the
dam of the South Fork Keeervoir, and that
there is such strong euspicn n of such
violence or other unlawful acts as to make an
inqaest necessary.

np with dynamite this afternoon. This is
the church which caught fire on that

tower stood alone and was a constant
menace to passers-by. It was condemned
and danger sigoals placed near it, but as a
measure of salety the authorities ordered
it to be demolished.

caught in the river at Warsaw, Kentucky,
yesterday, supposed to be from Johnstown.
The bodies of animals.and a cart were also

JOHNSTOWN DISASTER.
A Large Number of Bodies Still Being
Found.
Johnstown, June 9. - This is the tenth
day since the disaster in the Conemaugh
valley occurred, and the extent of the
fatality can be appreciated when it is
known that bodies are still beiug found
wherever men are at work. To-day one of
the morgue directors was met and asked
the usual question, "How many bodies {
were recovered to day ?" He replied :
"There were fifty-eight altogetheer." The ,
remains that are now being removed from \
the drift are far advanced in decomposi- J
Hod, and the physicians in charge are
advocating their cremation as fast as found,
as it is almost impossible to hold them
safriy. The work of clearing away the !

debris is progressing very encouragingly.
The workmen were not required to pro- j
ceed to-day but nine tenths of them volun- i
teered to continue the work. As a result a
large inroad was made on the drift in the i
central portion of the city. Main street
was the principal thoroughfare and was
one vast blockade, but it is now about
cleared of the wreckage. Above the stone
bridge the work is going on very slowly,
but the force is small and the difficulties
are great. Mr. Arthur Kirk who has been
using dynamite blasts to separate the drift
suspended operations to-day. A
considerable force continued to use the pike poles
and cleared a few feet more. Ex-Internal
Revenue Collector Bigler, of the western
Pennsylvania district, said to-day to an
Associated Press reporter, that if he were
given permission he conld bring in 200

practical cant hook men from Clearfield
lumber districts and clean the channel
above the bridge in two days. The trouble
with those at work is that they lack the
experience. He mentioned the matter to
Adjutant General Hastings, but did not
meet with very mnch enconragement.
This has been a very quiet day in and
about Johnstown, owing to the fact that
the Pennsylvania and Baltimore & Ohio
railroads refused to run trains from
Pittsburg or other important points nearer than
Bolivar on the former and Rockwood on
the latter road. This role kept ont a large
influx of excursionists and left the field
clear to the workers. Religious services
were held at various points to day, and in
mo.-t of the suburban towns where church
buildings remain regular services were
held. In Johnstown open air meetings
were held at different points. This has

bec-n the hottest day since the disaster and
the weather istellingon the workmen. With
fires that are constantly kept going
burning up the rubbish and the hot sun many
of them were exhausted before evening.
The hot sun beating down on the
wreckage above the bridge has developed the
fact that many bodies of animals and
probably human beings are yet in ti e rains.
The stench arising from this pile has been
more offensive to day than any time yet.
Drunkenness Responsible for Many
Who Were Drowned.

Detroit, Jane 10. - A. S. Hatch,
superintendent of the Electric Light works at
Johnstown, says liquor is responsible for
the loss of at least 3,000 lives during the
flood. He says after the water invaded the
first floors men invaded the saloons and at
the time of the great wave nearly a
thousand dranken men were on the streets.
They were nnable to save themselves and
caught and dragged others down; moreover,
their families were drowned for lack of
their assistance.
Statue Unveiled.
Rome, June 9. - The statue of Bruno was
unveiled to-day with imposing ceremonies.

Thirty thousand persons, including
students and deputations from varions parts
of Italy, marched in procession through
the principal streets. The removal of the
canvass covering from the statue was the
signal for deafening cheers. The
ceremonies were witnessed by thesyndec of Rome,
government officials and a large nnmber of
senators and deputies. Deputy Bovio, in
an oration, enlogized the martyr and
declared to-day there was born a religion of
free thought and liberty of conscience which
would be worse for papacy that the loss of
temporal power. The proceedings
throughout were orderly. The memory of
Garibaldi was honored with imposing
ceremonies to-day.

The Pope's Condition.
Rome, Jane 9. - The Pope is mnch
depressed. It is reported that he refuses to
see anybody and that he has passed three
days in prayer in his private chapel. Four
hundred telegrams have arrived at the
Vatican deploring the unveiling of the
Brnno monument. All the ambassadors
accredited to the Vatican met this evening
in the Pope's chapel. King Hnmbert
congratulated the ministers on the absence of
disorder. ___

10. - [Special.] - Adjutant-General Alger and his staff, at noon

Accompanying General Alger were Governor
Lnce and staff, the members of the
commission under whose direction the

Smith and Curtis.

passed through Port Leyden and adjacent 1
country yesterday afternoon, overturning
houses, trees and fences and damaging

EFFECTS OF THE FLOOD.
Railroads, Mills and Houses Swept
Away.
Huntington, Pa., Jnne 5. - Late news
from the suburban districts of this county
shows that the destruction to property by
the flood is infinitely greater than at first
reported. The waters are receding, and
couriers have arrive^ bearing news of
unprecedented floods from Bedford to
HuntiDgton on the Roystown brauch aud on to
Lewistown on the Juniata river. The
devastation is greatest in central
Pennsylvania, excepting, of course, Johnstown.

Not a house is left that stood within
reach of the swollen streams. Here the
damage to property will reach $500,000,
while other towns in the county have
suffered proportionately. At Mapleton the
immense tannery of L. A. Roberts was
damaged to the extent of $ 200 , 000 , and
the loss to other property will reach $ 100
,000 more. The Powell furnace at Saxton
sustained a loss of $300,000, aDd at that
place both railway bridges were Bwept
away, leaving railroad communication
with Bedford cut off For a distance of
four miles below here the Pennsylvania
tracks are destroyed, with the bridges
gone at Manayunk and Lewiston, the
latter goiDg down daring the heavy storm
last night. Growing crops in the low
lands were destroyed, and in Smith's
valley, this county, farming lands comprising
an area of twelve by two miles has been

stripped of every vestige of soil. As far
as known 300 houses have been destroyed
in this county. Three families, comprising
sixteen people, living on the Royston
branch, are missing and it is feared they
have been swept away by the flood.
AT JOHNSTOWN.
From 9,000 to 12,000 Supposed to be
Lost.
Johnstown, June 5. - As the days roll
on and the heaps of debris are penetrated,
it becomes more and more apparent that
the death list will be more than 5,000, and
the general impression is that the victims
will nnmber from between 9,000 to 12,000.

The deeper the wreck drifts are penetrated
the greater are the nnmber discovered.
On Franklin avenue 11 were found
today, and a few minutes afterward 12 more
were found.
Dr. Leeds, the Pennsylvania State
Board of Health representative, was to-day
asked what was his opinpin about the
prospects of an epidemic in Conemaugh
valley. He said : "God only knows. No
man living can tell what will come out of
these piles of drift aud wreckage. To-day
we started a portion of our corps of
sanitary inspectors into the thick of the debris
and in a little while the bodies of 50 dead
animals - mostly horses - had been removed
and hauled away for burial. If this
percentage is kept up here there is a fearful
amount of decomposing animal matter to
be removed or encountered. I have to-day
ordered the Snrgeon General at
Washington to forward unlimited quantities of
disinfectants to Johnstown. There is more

promise from np the mountain, and I hope
to be able to have the whole city fortified
inside of a few days."

the work at Stone bridge to day has been

Opposed to Strikes.
Chicago, June 5 - The Evening Journal
says: There is tronhle in the ranks of the
Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers.
Chief Arthur is a candidate for re election,
and as such is making a quiet canvass of
tbe varions lodges of the brotherhood. Last
week a secret meeting for this purpose was
held in this city. There were upward of
200 members present, and with their de
feat by the "Q" momentarily expected, a
reduction of wages on the Santa Fe and
the recent discharge by the Alton of a
large number of brotherhood men fresh in
their minds, they were not at all satisfied
with the chief 's optimistic speech.
Members of t e grievance committee, address

iug Chief Arihnr, said: A reduction of wages
is expected t<> be made before long on a
number of Western roads. Such action
we do not propose to accept, because we do
not believe it justified. We therefore
desire to know whether io the event of a
redaction being ordered, despite our
opposition, yon would sanction a strike.
Chiet Arthur did not like the question,
but saw there was no help for it and
answered: "Under no condition of circnm
stancs of which I can conceive shall I ever
sanction another strike." "But, sir," broke
in the questioner, "suppose a reduction of
wages should occur on the Union Pacific
system, where the Brotherhood is so
thoroughly equipped as to the obtaining
and granting of anything they ask, would
not you authorize a strike to resist it?"
Without a moment's hesitation Chief
Arthur replied "No, sir, I would not. I trust

and I believe that no reduction of wages is
to he made, but should there be and the
men follow my advice they will accept the
redaction. I shall never sanction another
strike." Chief Arthur then stopped and
the meeting adjourned. Murmurs of
discontent have been heard ever since. It was
known that the Chief bad a strong dislike
for strikes, bat that his conservatism was so
extreme as his Bpeech gave it to be was
never dreamed of.

POSTAL AFFAIRS.
Circular in Hegard to the Railway
Mail Service*
Washington, June 10. - The following
general circular was issued this evening
from the Postoffice Department :
In connection with the future
management of the railway mail service, the
general superintendent wishes to convey
to those eogaged in it his determination to
advance its efficiency and usefulness, the
accomplishment of which can only lie
attained by the earnest and intelligent
cooperation of the superintendents and postal
clerks. Every ODe attached to the
organization will be expected to perform his fall
duty, closely observing and obeying the
postal laws and regulations, as well as
orderb and instructions that from time to
time are issued for his information and
guidance. A partial enforcement
of the discipline of the service
will not be satisfactory ; neither can
excuses be accepted for neglect of duty;
for irregularities resulting from
carelessness or inattention nor for misdemeanors of

any kind. Clerks are required to keep
themselves posted upon the distribution
assigned to them; to be familiar with the
schedule of connections and with the book
of instructions; to study the weekly
bulletin ot general orders prepared in each
division, and to closely examine and note
special orders issued by those who have
authority over them. It is the present
belief that instructions relating to
checking of errors are not strictly followed, aud
it is supposed, in maLy instances, that
clerks have agreed among themselves not to
check each other,thus defeatiegthe purpose
of one of the most essential methods which
have been instituted for the betterment of
the service. It should be understood that
measures will be taken to ascertain who
disregard these orders, and to replace them
with those who are more diligent and
faithful. To those who perform their duty,

and by their capability and interest merit
advancement, every condition will be given
in the filling of advanced positions.
Particular attention in selecting for promotion
will be paid to the records for efficiency in
distribution, obedience to orders, and good
moral character.
J. Lowbie Bell, Gen Sapt.

Johnstown, June 5. - The temperature
remains low in the Conemaugh valley, and its
benefits are inestimable and should it
continue a lew days longer it is probable that

The work of clearing up the wreck and

systematically. Over 6,000 men are at work in
the valley. As the rubbish is gone over

recovered, tbe debris is piled upaud the torch

RESPONSIBILITY FOR THE DISASTER
in Old Resident Says - He
Where the Blame Rests.
Tells
Johnstown, June 6. - Thomas Jacobs,
of Morrelville, is one of the oldest
inhabitants of the Conemaugh valley. He said,
to-day, that the water of the river was
much higher in 1837 than last Friday,
even after the dam broke.

"The whole trouble about this deplorable
affair," he continued, "seems to be froa
the narrowing of the channel of the river
and the deflection ef its natural course. I
remember well when the channel ran down
where the mill below the bridge now stands.
The Conemaugh has always been a shallow
stream. After a heavy rainfall it rises
rapidly as all mountain streams do. Its
speed is great, and the hillsides so
constructed that the water runs down rapidly
and raises turbulent currents.
"Primarily I hold the Cambria Iron Co.,
as responsibe for the narrowing of the
channel, anci secondly the South Fork club for
not having made the dam secure beyond
all possibility of a break, when they caused
the dam to be enlarged by raising the
breast; and, thirdly, the Pennsylvania
railway for having constructed a viaduct with

such low arches and with ribs likely to
catch pieces of drift wood if they happen to
strike diagonally on the piers. The dam
made by the George bridge is what engulfed
the town. '

The Number of Dead from 12,000 to 15,000
Over Half the Number Recovered.
Johnstown, Pa., June 3. - The rescuing
parties at work on the mass of unburied
wreckage in the river, are finding bodies and
fragments at ten to fifteen an hour. In
ether parts of the submerged district maoy
bodies are being taken out.
A careful estimate of the bodies recovered
everywhere puts it at 7,000 to 8,000.
The bodies of Patrick Hogan, wife, and
children, were found in the debris, partly
horned, this morning. In one of the few
remaining houses in Johnstown, tbiB
morning, the searchers found and rescued a man
so weak that he could not give his name.

Forty-eight bodies now at Johnstown
station, will be buried as fast as possible.
Very few have been identified. Fifty men
are digging graves on Prospect Hill.
The latest from Connemaugh says that
but four were lost of those on the
unfortunate train caught in the flood at the
bottom of the bill. These were in the Pullman
sleeper.
HUNDREDS OF BODIES
are lying on the sand at Kernville, this
afternoon. A-crowd of 500 is gathered
around endeavoring to find the bodies of
friends or rotatives. Mo coffins are there,
but E00 are on the way here, and the
undertakers sent fer 500 additional.
Kernville, from now on, will be the place where
most of the bodies will be found under a
pile of debris about an acre in length.

Rain is now falling but it does not
interfere with the work. Most of the rescuing
party have been up two days.
The fire at the bridge is almost
extinguished, and the task of getting at the
bodies under the bnrning debris will be

THE TOTAL LOSS OF LIFE.
The water has subsided to a great extent
and the streets in the main part of town
are free from water. The falling water has
laid bare tbe terrible work of tbe flood,
and the full extant of the disaster is only
being ascertained now. The streets are a
sickening, foul-smelling mass of wood and
debris, and the ftork of searching ior
bodies has only fairly begun.

The latest estimates place the loss of life
at from 10,000 to 12,000. It is
impossible to get any account of those lost.
Every one is so thoroughly tired out and
overcome by the weight of the disaster as
to be utterly unable to give any accurate
details or figures. Comparatively few
have been identified.

Wyoming to Try Statehood.
Cheyenne, Wyo. T., June 3. - Governor
Warren, to-day, issued a proclamation for
an election on July 8, of delegatee to a
constitutional convention. The governor,
secretary and chief justice had previously
divided the territory into districts and
apportioned the delegates among the same.
This action was taken in response to tbe
request of the commissioners of nearly all
of the counties in Wyoming, and is in
accord with the views of the prominent
citizens without regard to party. Wyoming
has the population, wealth and public
intelligence to entitle it to immediate
admission, and its people will earnestly appeal
to Congress to that end.

TAKEN UNDER ADVISEMENT.
Judge De Wolfe Withhold« Hi» Decision
in the Case of the Doctor».

Aside from bearing a few minor motions
the attention of Judge De Wolfe was
occupied the entire afternoon yesterday in
bearing arguments on demurrers against the
indictments returned against Drs. Harding,
Weyerhorst, Schultz and Beale, for
unlawfully practicing medicine in the territory.
The demurrers are not only against the
indictments themselves, which it is claimed
are wrongly drawn up, but also against the
validity of the law establishing the board
of medical examiners and regulating the
practice of medicine in the territory.
Messrs. McBride & Haldorn and Messrs.

Scallon, Speer and Keithly appeared for
the doctors and Mrs. McConnell and
Stapleton for the medical board, which, of
course, is contending that the law is valid
and constitutional. Should the court so
decide, then the cases will come up for trial
on the indictments.
When all arguments had been heard
Judge De Wolfe announced that he would
take the matter under advisement and
withhold decision for a few days. In the
meantimes both sides will submit more
authorities on the question.

It is now conceded that the great

blessing to the city, as it has cleared out all
the old tinder box structures that were a
constant menace to the safety of the

a calamity as this, and the city will

unknown.

Death of a Former Resident.
Francis Farnum, an esteemed and
highly respected citizen of Danbury.died
of pulmonary consuamption June 6.
Deceased was born in Concord, west of
Long Pond, October 19, 1820. He lived
in Concord until four years subs:quent
to his marriage with Amanda Abbott,
also of Concord, when he removed to
Danbury, in 1854, where he has since
resided.
Mr. Farnum, in company with his
brother, John C. Farnum, while a resi- |
dent of Concord, furnished and laid the '
stone foundation of the present
county jail. He led a very
active business life. characterized to a
remarkable degree by quietness, and an
amiable bearing toward all classes of
persons with whom he came in contact.

Mr. Farnum was conscientious and
upright in character, 8 fond husband and
father, ever caring for the welfare of his
family. Sadly will a wife, three sons
and three daughters miss his presence.
He had been yielding gradually to lung
disease. but bore with quiet fortitude the
disabilities and self sacrifice forced
upon him by failing health, and with
unyielding courage he attended to his
'business until very near the close of his
life, which was quiet and peaceful.
heleaves a large circle of relatives
widely scattered, though many of them
reside in Concord and vicinity. Funeral
services, conducted by Elder Morrill,
were held at his late residence,
Saturday, June 8. i

Details of a horrible double
murder which occurred near the village of
Meriden, early Tuesday morning,
reached this city by telephone Tuesday
forenoon. All the facts so far obtaimable
are these: Lucian Freeman, about 35
yeaas of age, killed his mother and a man
named John Morgan, a resident of the
same town, with an ax at the home of
the former and disappeared. From a
representative in the legislature it has been
learned that Freeman Is insane and
had been cared for by Morgan, who
was at his house for that purpose.

The body of Morgan was found in bed
with the head nearly or quite decapitated,
while that of Mrs. Freeman was
discovered lying upon the floor near the
front door. It is presumed that Morgan,
considered that Freeman's condition was
comfortable enough to warrant his
(Mor'gan's) retiring, which he did, and that
'during the night the insane man arose,
secured an ax and made an attack upon
'him with the fatal results stated. It is
probable that Mrs. Freeman, hearing the
noise, attempted to escape from the
'house, but was overtaken by the
frenzied man and killed. The murderer fled
in his night clothes, and went to the
house of a Mr. Eaton at East Plainfield,
a distance of four miles, where he was
taken in and put to bed, and a son of Mr.

Eaton was sent to Meriden to inform
Fred Freeman of his brother's
whereabouts. Much alarmed, Fred hurried to
his mother's house, and upon looking in
at a window discovered her lying dead
upon the floor, and upon a bed in
another room was Mr. Mox;ian also dead.
An inquest was held at the town hall in
Meriden Tuesday afternoon, before
Coroner Otis F. i Waite of Claremont,
with *J:' T. Duncan, D.- N. Moulton,

and W. P. Wood as jurymen. Several
persons were examined, and the jury
rendered a verdict holding Freeman for
murder. He will be taken to the
county jail at Newport, to await trial in
September, unless he shall be committed so
the insane asylum at Concord at an
earlier date by order of the court.

AID FOR JOHNSTOWN,
A cry for help comes from Johnstown,
where the fearful flood did its awful work
of devastation. The cry should not be
unheeded. Every littie helps. Pawtucket,
always generous, should not be the last to
respond to the call.
Victims perished by thousands.
Husbands were torn from wives, parents from
children, lovers from sweethearts and
friends from friends. Engulfed in one
common death, they perished in sight of
each other, unable to help themselves,
powerless to give warning to those who
might thus have been saved, hurried along
by a swirling rush of water which drowned
and strangled and bore ite victims like
debris upon its bosom, as though possessed
by a congcious spirit of vindictive slaughter.

Let the appeal of the survivors be not in
vain.

prlrsrne., Pa., June 1.-One of the
most appalling calamities that ever
occurred in this country has just resulted
frnom the breaking of the great reservoir
above Johnstown, Pa., about 5 o'clock
last evening. The reservoir lies about 18
miles northeast of Johnstown. It was
formerly known as Conemaugh lake, in
the Allegheny mountatns. It is three
and a half miles long and a mile and a
quarter in width. It was about 100 feet
deep and holds more water than,any oth
er reservoir, natural or artificial, in the
United States.

The lake has been quadrupled in size
by artificial means and it was held in
check by a dam 700 to 1,000 feet wide.
It is ninety feet in thickness at the base
and the hesght is 110 feet. The top has
a breadth of over twenty feet.
Reccoguizing the menace which the lake
presented to the region below, the South
Fork club, which owned the reservoir,
had the dam inspected once a month by
a Pennsylvania railroad engineer and
their investigation showed that nothing
less than some convulsion of nature
would tear the barrier away and loosen
the weapon of death. The steady rains
of the past forty-eight hours increased
the volume of water in all the small
mountain streams, which were already
swelled by lesser rains earlier in the
week. From the information obtained at
this time it is evident something in the

nature of a cloud burst must have been
the culmination of the struggle of the
water against the embankment.
The course of the torrent from the
broken dam at the foot of the lake to
Johnstown is almost eighteen miles, and
with the exception of one point the
water passel through a narrow V-shaped
valley. Four miles below the dam lay
the town of South Fork. where the South
Fork itself empties into the Conemaugh
river. The town contained about 2,000
inhabitants. It has not been heard from
but it is said four-fifths of it has been
swept away. Four miles further down
on the Conemaugh river, which runs
parallel with the main line of the
Pennsylvania railway, was the town of Mineral
Point. It had 800 inhabitants, 90 per
cent of the houses being on a flat and
close to the river. It seems impossible

at this time to hope that any of them
have escaped. Six miles further down
the stream was the town of Conemaugh,
and here alone there was a topographical
possibility of the spreading of the flood
and the breaking of its force. It
contained 2,500 inhabitants and must be
almost wholly devasted. Woodvale, with
2,000 people, lay a mile below Conemaugh
in a flat and one mile further down were
Johnstown and its cluster of sister towns,
Cambria City and Conemaugh, with a
total population of 30,000. On made
ground and stretched along the river
were the inmmense iron works of the
Cambria Iron and Steel Co., who have
$5,000,000 invested in their plant.
Besides this there are many other large
industrial establishments on the banks of
the river. How badly damaged they are
ca.nnot be estimated.

The tracks west of Johnstown are at
some points entirely carried away and the
roadbed is gone. The river for some
distance above the bridge is filled with
buildings and driftwood forty feet high, which
is on fire and likelyto damage the bridge,
which is of stone. The fire is beyond
contr 1. Johnstownis literally wiped out.
Watchers with lanterns remained along
the banks until day broke, when the first
view of the awful devastation of
the flood was witnessed. Here and
there were uprooted trees and piles of
drift lay about :in which some of the
bodies of the victims will be found.
Rescuing parties are being formed along the
railroad. ilouses have been thrown open
for the refugees and every possible means
is being used to protect the homeless. A
courier from the scene of the flood near

Johnstown reports that the loss of life
will reach 1,500.
A conductor reports that immediately
after his train has passed over the bridge
which spans the river at South Fork that
structure was swept away by the rushing
water.
A boy who" was almost miraculously
saved, relates the following story of what
he saw of the frightful calamity:
"With my father I was spending the
day at my grandfather's house in Cambria
City. In the house at the time were
Theodore Enwart and John King, jr.,Mrs.

iMary King, the wife of John jr., Miss
Tracy Oing, Mrs. Rico Smith, John
Hirsch and four children, father and
myself. Shortly after 5 o'clock there was a
noise of roaring waters and screams of
people. We looked out the door and saw
people running. My father told us to
never mind, the waters would rise no
further; but we soon saw houses swept
away and then ran up stairs. The house
was three stories, and we were at last
forced to the top floor. In my fright I
jumped on a bed. It was an old
fashioned one with wooden posts. The water
kept rising and my bed was soon
floatiu,. Gradually it was lifted up. The
air in the room grew close and the house
was moving. Still the bed kept pressing

the ceiling. At last the posts pushed the
plaster, it yielded and a section of the
roof gave way. Then suddenly I found
myself on the roof and was being carried
down stream. After a little this roof
commenced to part and I was afraid I was
going to be drowned, but just then
,another house with a shingle roof floated by
and I managed to crawl onto it and
floated down until, nearly dead with cold, I
was saved. After I was free from the
house I did not see my father. My
grandfather was in a tree, but he must
have been drowned, as the water was
rising. John King was also in a tree. Miss
Mary King and Mrs. Mary King I saw
drown. Miss Smith was also drowned.

John Hirsch was in a tree, but the four
children were drowned. The scenes were
terrible. People and corpses were
floatuing down with me and away from me. I
would hear a person shriek, and then
they would disappear. Along the line
were-people who were trying to save us,
but they could do nothing, and only a
few were caught."
Horror Upon Horrors.
NEw FLORENCE, June 1,-"How can
anybody tell how many are dead?" was
asked of a railroad engineer this
morning. "1 have been at Snag Hollow since
11 o'clock yesterday and seen fully 500
persons lost in the flood." The most
dreadful culmination of the awful night
was the roasting of a hundred or more
persons In Milford by fire, the ruins of
houses and out buildings and other
structures swept against the new railroad
bridge at Johnstown, and from an
overturned stove or some other cause the
upper part of the wreckage caught fire.

There were crowds of men, women and
children on the wreck. Their screams
added to the awful chorus of horror; they
were literally roasted in the flood. The
first authentic news is from W. H. Hayes
of the Pennsylvania R. R. Co., who
reached New Florence at 9 o'clock. He says
the valley towns are annihilated.
The Sufferers by the Flood.
WASHINGTON, June 1.-There is no
communication wi-h the South either by
railroad or telegraph, because of storms.
The resignation of F. M. Stockslayer,
commissioner of the general land office,
tendered March 5th last, was today
acaccepted by the president to take effect
June 30. Gen. Scofield, acting secretary
of war, asked Gov. Beaver by telegraph,
what the war department can do to aid
the flood sufferers in Pennsylvania. He
says the department has no tents; all
extra ones having been sent to Charleston

during the earthquake and never
returned.
Heartrending Scenes.
PIHLADELPHIA, Pa., June 1.--At 1:30
this morning news was received from
Bolivar stated that two story houses,
barns, stables, whole forests of trees,
outhouses, smoke-houses, railroad bridges,
county bridges, rafts, inverted skiffs and
driftwood by the acre were floating
byfrom all of which imploring hands were
stretched out to those on the banks,
willing but impotent to help. At Lockport,
two miles east, twenty persons have been
taken from the flood.
Fearful Flood of Death.
NEw FLORENCE,' Pa., June 1.-One
hundred bodies have been recovered at
Nineveh; 70 persons are reported burned
to death in the fire at Johnstown
bridges. Wm. Hays has just returned from
Johnstown and says the place is
annihilated; Conemaugh is wrecked and
Cambria City is swept away. Fully 1,500
lives are lost.

Three Thousand Souls Swept Away.
PITTsBUcio, June 1.-Persons
returning from the scenes of the disaster say at
least 3,000 have lost their lives. Men,
women and children were carried along
frantically shrieking for help, but rescue
was impossible. Husbands were swept
past their wives and children were borne
along at a terrible speed to certain death
before the eyes of their frantic parents.
The Packers Combine.
KANSAS CITY, June 1.-The interstate
commerce commission concluded its
hearings here on the question of difference in
rates between live hogs and the dressed
product. The Chicago board of trade
favored Kansas City packers and opposed
the equalization of rates.

West Point Graduation.
POUGHKEHSIE, N. Y., June 1.-The
annual examination at West Point military
academy began today. The members of
the first class will be graduated on the
12th under the trees in front of the
academy library.
Measures for Relief.
PrrrsnuRo, June 1.-A citizens
meeting has been called to advise means to
aid the sufferers of the Johnstown flood.

TO CELEBRATE THE FOURTH OF

Stray Notes from the Capital.
HELENA, June 1, 1889.-[Special to the
LEADER.]-Helena is the boom building
town of the west-and nothing more. A
great deal of real estate changes hands,
but it is principally between real estate
agents who place it at fictitious prices in
order to catch the pilgrim. In
conversation with a gentleman today about the
"great building boom" he remarked thist
he could see nothing in the
surroundings to justify it. But, he said, the
"boom" is here and the people are
making the most of it. How long it will last
I don't know, but the end will come and
great will be the crush. History will
repeat itself right here in Helena, and don't

you forget it.
It is said that Billy Todd of the
Benton Press has the inside track in the
race for the chief clerkship of the
constitutional convention. Billy has labored
faithfully for the unwashed combination
and should be awarded.
Grand preparations are being made for
the celebration here on the Fourth of
July. Major General Col. Charles
Dennis Curtis, postmaster of Helena and
general handy man on all such occasions,
has been appointed marshal of the day.
There is no dobbt but that the Colonel
will select a brilliant staff of aids which
will be worth a journey from Miles City
to Helena to look at. It is the intention
of the committee having the celebration
in charge to make it one of the grandest
events of the age. The people of the
whole territory are expected to be
present and take part in the exercises. As

the constitutional convention assembles
on that day a double interest will be
added to the occasion. The program will
be announced in a few days. It is said
that preparations are in progress for the
accommodation of 30,000 visitors.
The many friends of Paris Gibson in
this city would like to see him made
presiden of the constitutional
convention. It is hinted by some that Paris
would rather hold off and become the
democratic candidate for governor. The
unwashed of Cascade should not kick at
this.

It is currently reported in society
circles that Judge Bach of Great Falls will
cut loose from the life of single
blessedness that he has been leading for the
past twenty-five years and lead to the
altar on the 6th of June, the pretty and
accomplished Miss Child, sister of II. \V.
Child, manager of the smelter. This is
right, judge. The Good Book says it is
not good for man to live alone.
The address of Major Maginnis
delivered at Great Falls on Decoration l)ay,
as reported in the LEADER, is highly
spoken of as is master piece of eloquence.

The major can talk to the point when he
gets among the boys that "drank from the
same canteen" in the sixties.
Decoration Day services in Hlelena were
elaborate and impressive. Business was
generally susplended and all joined in
doing honor to the memory of the deed
heroes. The speeches of Chief Justice
Blake of Helena and Rev. 3McMillan of
Deer Lodge were eloquent and fitting to
the occasion.
Deputy Sheriff IHamilton, II. P. Rolfe,
Dr. Crutcher, J. L. Henry and several
other prominent denizens of Great Falls
were in the city the past week on
business.

Nick Kessler has sold his brewery,
located at this place, for $350,000.
It is reported that John Maguire has
accepted the management of. the San
Francisco theatre and will leave in a short
time to assume his duties. It will be
hard to find a man to fill his place in
Montana.
The great flood at Jlohnstown, Pa., has
cast a gloom over the city as many of our
people had friends and relatives in that
section.
Reports from the surrounding country
say that the crops look remarkably well
considering the absence of snow and the
small rainfall.

It will not be many moons ere the real
estate men of HIelena will begin to
emigrate. A good many of them have their
right eye on Great Falls as the coming
city of Montana.
Mr. Don Davenport and Miss Bessie

to Death
Near Cascade, Mt., on
Friday Night!
[From our Extra of yesterday morning.]
CASCADE, Mont., June 1, 1889,
noon.[Special to the LEADE.I.]--A dreadful
calamity occurred here last night,
resulting in the burning to death of Capt.
George W. (:ad g :tthe early settlers
of Montana and one of our most highly
respected citizens.
Capt. Cadge came to Montana about
fifteen years ago. He had been a sea
captain, sailing out of English and
American ports, for twenty-five years prior to
removing to Montana.

He was married in New York city in
the fall of 1888--his bride, a highly
accomplished and lovely young lady,coming
from England to meet him there.
lie was from one of the best English
families and was a most genial, generous,
large-hearted and courteous
gentlemanrespected by all and beloved by the wide
circle of friends who knew of his nobility
of character.
He has been for years among the
leadine cattle-owners of the country; was a
Mason of high degree and identitfied with
many of the benevolent movements and
substantial enterprises of the territory;
was about seventy years of age, in the
prime of health and the bloom of
avigorous old age.

His dreadful death has cast such a pall
of gloom upon the community as we have
never before experienced.
LATER I)ISPATCH.
(CAScADE, June 1, 6 p. m.-[Special to
the LEADIst.]}--Near midnight. last night
the residence of ('apt. George W. Cadge,
about 9 miles down the valley from here,
caught fire. He and his wife got up
and lie opened the door leading to the
room where the fire was,when the flamnes
rolled in upon himu. They at once
rushed out of another door. After getting
out he thought of some valuable papers
lie wished to save and went back to get
them, when he suffocated and fell. As
no one was there to help him lie was
soon caught in the rlames and burned.

Nothing but the trunk of his body
remnained.
Mr. A. Lamb, an employe, was
sleeping in another house near by, but when
he got there nothing could he done. Mr.
Jamles Travis, . r., with hisi family was also
about 200 yards distant; but the roof was
falling in when he got to the scene. He
and -Mr. Lamb carried water and
extinguished the tire sutlicient to get the ,bdy
out, which was nearly burned up and hor
rible to behold. An inquest is to be held
today.
Capt. t(. W. Cadge was an old sea
captain, lhaving been master of ships to
prominsent ports of the world.

About 15 years ago he came to
Montana and took up the land where he lost
his life. lie also entered the stock business
and by economy and industry, coupled
with honesty, lie made a fortlune.
With his wife hie had been living in
Helena; but they had just got their ranch
house fitted up to make it their future
home and had only been living in it a
little over a month.
D)eceased was a man nearly (10 yeatrs
old and has hie iti a prominent netnlber of
the masonic body for years. The loss is
deeply felt in the community where lhe
has lived so long.

Special Dispatch to the Dally Eazle.
Guthrie, Ok., June 3. The first serious
infraction of the law in Guthrie occurred
last night at midnight, when one or more
burglars entered a tent in the north part
of the city occupied by Dr. Sebring and
Seth" Clark, robbing them of their money
and inflicting serious injury upon Sebring.
Jlr. Sebring was formerly a resident of
Kingman, Kan., where he was engaged in

the livery business. He is also said to
have been proprietor of a saloon there at
one time, aud Seth Clark was in his
employ as bartender. The two in company
with Scbring's brother, Joseph, and one or
two others came to Guthrie April 22 and
located lots. Several days ago Sebring
disposed of his lot but reserved the privilege
of occupying his tent as a sleeping plapo.
Mr. Clark, who occupied the teut with
liim, says that he out in town until 10
o'clock last evening and on returning to
retire found Sebring asleep. He can give
no account ot the tragedy except that ho
awoke some time in the night in a half
dazed condition and heard some
threatening remarks made and then relapsed
into an unconscious state. J. M. Suits,
who occupied an adjoining tent, heard

what he at first presumed was two men
quarreling. He thought, although he
could not hear the conversation, that two
acquaintances were engaged in a
dispute, but soon he heard serious
threats made. A shot was fired
followed by the noise. of one or more
men leaving in a hurry. Mr. Suits ran to
a neighbor's house, procured u lantern
nnd in company with several other men
went to the tent and found Sebrinc
covered with blood. He was throwing his arms
wildly about him, but was unconscious.

He hud been shot in the left cheek with a
small calibre pistol, the ball ranging
downward. "He had also received several
blows on the face and head and a deep cut
on his left lea. It seems that he had

wrapped his money amounting to S115 in
his pocket handerchief and tied it around
his ankle. The robbers cut the
handkerchief and roll of money in two,
securing but half of each bill.
They albo took 10 from Clark's pockets,
which is the sole earnings for their
nisht's work. The city marshal has the
other half of-the severed bills.
Mr. Clark lay near his companion
apparently asleep and was aroused with
difficulty. 'J he only outward evidence that
lie had been roughly handled was that his
nose had been bleeding. Ho is now in the
city jail awaiting developments.

Considerable excitement prevails over
the election which is to come oil
tomorrow. A. V. Alexander, a prominent
Kansas lumberman, is Colonel Dyer's
opponent for mayor.
Later Word has arrived here that the
party who assaulted and robbed Sebring
lias been arrested at Alfred with the
missinc money in his possession.

XoRMAN, Ok., June 3. Xormnn was
laid out April 22, 1SSD, or rather was first

fettled on that memorable day. This
young and growing city, which indeed it
might justly be called, and richly deserves
to bo so called, now contains a population
of 500 inhabitants, and is most beautifully
situated on the Santa Fe railroad, eighteen
miles south of Oklahoma City and fifteen
miles north of Purcell. The town
is finely located in the midst of a level,
beautiful prairie of unequaled fertility.
The town is surrounded in the form of a
semicircle by a beautiful little creek,
charmingly fringed by small groves of
trees Interspersed by the tall trees ot the
forest.

Three miles southwest of the town flows
the magnificent river known as the South
Canadian, on whose banks is an
abundance of fine timber.
The country naturally tributary to
TCorman for its commercial and
mechanical suppl es embraces a tract of country
westward twenty miles wide, north nnd
south and littv miles west, extending to

ward the town of Norman will command
the trade and business of a level, rich and
most deliehtful country: in extent twenty
miles from north to south and to the Little

river on tho east, twentv-five miles dis
tant. The trade of the Iowa, Sac and Fox
Indians and the Shawnee Indians, as well
as the Pottawatomie Indians, will
naturally be directed to Norman, the Indians in
the country to trade with Norman having
no large river or streams to cross in going
there and havinir level roads all the way.

The town of Norman is under a safe and
most admirable government, no
disreputable places nor saloons being allowed to
exist in the tOAvn,nor probably ever will be
tolerated there, as the citizens are
distinguished for their opposition to such
things. They are a strictly a church-loving
and church-going people, as evinced
by the fact that the Catholic, Methodist
Episcopal, Methodist Episcopal church
south, Cumberland Presbyterian church
and Christian church have each secured

two lotB on which to build houses of
divine worship. As evidence of the
christian character of the citizens of Norman,
on Sunday, May 20, three sermons were
delivered successively by two ministers of
the gospel of the Methodist Episcopal
church south and one by a minister of the
Christian church.
The meeting alluded to was held in a
livery stable, reminding the followers of
Jesus that the Savior first made His ap

pearance on earth in a manger. No such
an occurrence as this ever transpired
before in Oklahoma territory nor ever likely
will again. The stable is not yet occupied
and wab furnished with seats, and all
things were conducted in order.
Norman is at once to have a new
railroad depot, and it is rumored it will be an

important railroad town ueiore long,

The principal streets of Norman

au sixty feet wide. The principal streets

murder of Charlie Palmer, near Emit, I.
T., on May 25. The case is a peculiar one,
aue to prove that tho Moore's killed Pal

mer will also develope the iact that the
killed a young man named Monroe
Kamp who mysteriously disappeared
about a year ago.

home from a mill, and the evidence
circumstantial, though strong, is that Tom
Moore killed him because he was assisting
in the investigation of the disappearance
of Kamp.

Among the People in the Devastated
Valley,
With Small Prospects of Breakfast
This Morning.
Women and Children Crouching
Shelterless on the Wreck.

Illation's Bounty.

the Dam.

in the Center,

Little Children In a Majority Among
the Victims.
Johnstown, Pa., June 5. - The best
estimates today on the loss of life, based
on the registry of the living and on an
unofficial poll, put it at from 12,000 to 15,000.

It must be remembered that a very large
proportion of this loss is made up of
children. How strikingly frequent ils the
reference in the death list to "Mrs. Jones and six
children," "Mrs. Smith and five children."
In the morgue the little ones lie in dozens
where the adults are in half-dozens, but
there is, and iias been, a much greater
difficulty in recovering the bodies of the
children. lleing lighter aud smaller, they have
often been swept into out-of-the way
recesses and carried away. A very great
proportion of the children have been swept down
the river, aDd their bodies driven under

overhanging banks, under thickets and other
places, where the search Is not carried on in
a careful and organized manner.
YESTERDAY'S SAD WORK.
The Crash of Dynamite Heard In the
Ruins.
It Makes Little Impression-One
Thousand Funerals With Few
Mournars-Men Wanted Who Can
Work - The Labor Systematized.
Johnstown, Pa., J~ne 5. - There is no

suict-Hsu ui uorrors u» B i me situation is
resolving Itself into k E (thing like order
and relief work is so ' systematized that
there is no danger lotat onfusion. At the
several distributing t. ,";s hundreds
assemble at morning, noon and night, and
forming In line are supplied with provisions.
Men and women with families are given
bread, butter, cheese, ham, canned meats
and tea or coffee. Nine hundred army tents
from Ohio have been divided into two white
walled villages which afford shelter for
nearly 6000 homeless people. These villages are
policed and under the charge of Oen. Axline.

The action of the authorities yesterday in
consolidating ail the authority and resting it
in J. B. Scott of Pittsburg as dictator, was
received with favor on all hands. He has
taken hold with energy and has already
mapped out the work and assigned the
direction of its various portions to men equally
zealous. He has 2500 men at work and lias
called for 2500 more to whom he promises
work for 00 days at 82 per day and board.
Mr. Soott today said he proposed to clear
the town of all the wreckage and debris of
all descriptions and turn the town site over
to the citizens, when he has completed the
work, clean and free from obstructions of all
kinds.

Today Superintendent] Duncan, of the
Johnstown street railway, one of the
leading citizens of the place, declared that as
soon as the people recovered in a measure
from their dazed condition immediate
measures would be taken towards rebuilding.
This will be a gigantic and costly work, but
Mr. Duncan expects to see a new city spring
from the ruins of Johnstown. The work of
reconstructing the road bed and relaying the
tracks of the Pennsylvania road is being
pushed forward vigorously already, and
trains are running to the passenger station.

The construction trains also go considerably
further. The high embankment at the big
bend of the river which deflected the river
from its course on the fatal Friday and
was Anally washed away Itself was
reconstructed today.
Where Johnstown's principal stores stood
Friday are now pitched 1000 tents and
before tomorrow night the number will
probably be doubled. Under this shelter are
accommodated the members of the militia and
thousands of workmen
TRYING TO Cr.EAIt THE STREETS
of the wrecked city. Over 8000 men are thus
employed In Johnstown proper, about 1500
being regular street hands employed by con
tractors and the others volunteers. William
Flinn of Pittsburg arrived this morning and
at once took charge of the army of laborers,
He said, -It will take 10,000 men 30 days tc
clear the ground so that the streets will lx
passable and the work of rebuilding can lx

commenced. 1 am at a loss to know how tlx
work is to be done. This enthusiasm will
soon die out and the volunteers will want U
return home. It would take all summer foi
my men to do the work necessary. Step!
must be taken at once to furnish gangs ol
I workmen Tomorrow I shall send a commu
nlcatlon to the Pittsburg Chamber of Com
merce asking the different manufacturers o
the Ohio valley to take turns for a month o
1 so in furnishing reliefs of workmen. I shal
ask each establishment to stop work for i
week at a time and send all hands In charg
of the foreman and timekeeper. We wll
board and caie for them here. These gang
should come for a week at a time. No oi
£ ganlzatioc can be effected if workmen arrlv

and leave when they please."
The volunteers are doing noble work
' Nearly every town in Western Pennsylvanl
, is represented by from 10 to 100 men am
manv towns in Ohio and New York hav
, furnished their quota of laborers. Thes
volunteers are working with a will. All tb
' laborers were quartered tonight, some 1

barns and others in tents. When supper
was ready, long pine tables were crowded
with men. Btoves were erected in the open.
Gallons of coffee were heated In large wash
boilers. For one gang of men, seven boilers
full were emptied in naif an hour. Coffee,
bread and cheese were the fare tonight, but
more substantial rations will be given out
tomorrow. At dark, the valley became
quiet, the only noise being an occasional
challenge of a militiaman as he bade some
belated Individual obey the orders of the
sheriff and leave the city of the dead.

Johnstown is under martial law and laborers
only are wanted.
A radical and disagreeable change of
temperature since yesterday will be prolific of
much suffering and many Ills. The air Is
now keen and penetrating. This condition
is favorable to the workers, but unpleasant
for the houseless sufferers. Thinly clad
WOMEN AND CHILDREN ARK SHIVERING
under the eaves of every convenient
building. The sight of long relief trains rolling
into Johnstown over both railroads, from
every section of the country, almost every
hour of the 24, tends to make the observer
conclude that charity is not so rare as the
cynic philosophers would have us believe.

From East, West, North and South come
whole train loads of clothing and provisions,
accompanied by special messengers having
funds, and a large corps of volunteer
physicians, nurses and workers. Accompanying
the big Philadelphia relief train was a
special car occupied by a corps of surgeons,
equipped with a large outfit of instruments
and medicines.
The registration of survivors goes on not
so rapidly as yesterday. The total
registration to date is a trifle over 12,000 out of a to
tal estimated population of 35,000 to 40,000.

Allowance must be made for the large
numbers of survivors who sought refuge with
friends in other places as well as the many
who failed from ignorance or remission to
register. The falling off of today leads the
authorities to apprehend that their worst
fears will be realized and the death roll
mount well up into five figures.
The gray mists had scarcely arisen from
the hills this morning before a thusand
funerals were coursing their green sides.
There were no hearses and few mourners
and as little solemnity as formality. A
majority of the coffins were of rough pine and
the pall bearers strong ox teams, there being
generally six coffins to one team. The men
silently unloaded the burdens in the lap of
mother earth. No minister was there,
except a few faithful priests who followed
some mangled representatives of their faith

recovered were so mangled, bruised or
charred that identification was impossible.
All day long the corpses were hurried below
the groud. The unidentified bodies were
grouped on a high hill
WEST OF THE DOOMED CITY,
where the epitaph "Unknown," must do for
all. Hundreds of these graves have been
made already, and each day will increase the
proportion. The possibility of identification
diminishes every hour. Fires are raging
over the tangled graves of hundreds, and
the partial cremation of many bodies is
inevitable. Others are becoming so blackened in
contact with the debris, or through
putrefaction, that a grinning skeleton would show
as much resemblance to the persons in life
as they. Almost every stroke of the pick iu
some portions of the city today resulted iD
the discovery of another victim. Although
the funerals relieved the morgues of
the crush, before night they were as full of

dead as ever.
Every train into Johnstown was laden
with coffins, the better ones being generally
accompanied by friends of the dead. Men
could be seen staggering over the ruins with
caskets on their shoulders. [Several
stumbled and fell into the abounding man pits.
Over 100 men have been all day engaged in
an effort to clear a narrow' passage from the
death bridge upward through the sea of
debris which blocks the Conemaugii for
nearly half a mile. Every ingenuity known
to man was resorted to by this crew.
Dynamite was brought into requisition and at
frequent intervals, sticks, stones and logs
would fly high in the air. Gradually a few
of the heaviest timbers were demolished and
their fragments permitted to flow
downward through the center arch. At nightfall
the clear space above the bridge did not
exceed 60 feet in length and 40 feet width.

There are 25 acres to be cleared Is this way
and the task seems Interminable. Many
conservative minds recommend
THE USE OF THE TOUCH
in clearing the river. They are not among
the sufferers. When'.such counsels are heard
by the wives, children, sisters or brothers of
those who rest beneath this sea of flotsam
and jetsam, the suggestion meets with wild
objection and in deference to this
unreasoning mandate of grief, the herculean labor of
clearing the river by means of the dynamite
and derrick is persisted in. No hope
remains in calmer minds that this task can be
pursued to the end. The progress of today
is hardly discoverable, and ere two more
days have elapsed there is little doubt that
the emanations of the putrid bodies will
become so frightful as to drive the hardiest
workmen from the scene. Until that time

arrives there is no hope that this grief
stricken populace will abandon the
cherished hope of again gazing upon the forms of
loved ones whose lives went out in the fire
and flood Of the Conemaugh.
At the various relief stations today the
crowd of applicants continued from morning
until night and many of the needy were
_a i ._u tli_Vw.fl,«i

turn came and their little portion wa9
allotted to them. Hundreds of thousands of
dollars must pour into this stricken valley if
positive suffering aud privation be avoided.
Thousands of people are homeless and
thousands lost their all. Labor and
manufacturing of nearly every kind is at a
standstill and weeks or months must elapse
before the Cambria Iron Works and other
Industrial Institutions can possibly resume
and give employment to the thousands that
depend on them for support. Hundreds of
hungry people In the Conemaugh valley
have no certaiDty of breakfast tomorrow.

- A Huge Pile of Dirt Across the

Johnstown, June 5. - The investigations
of a reporter today show clearly that
the major part of whatever responsibility
may belong to human agencies for the
calamity that has desolated the Conemaugh valley
must be placed upon the South Fork Fishing
and Hunting Club, the association of
wealthyPittsburg gentlemen that has four or
five years past been endeavoring to establish
a sportsman's paradise at Conemaugh Lake.

When they leased the lake they closed the
waste gates, through which all the water
that had ever before accumulated in
Conemaugh Lake had found a safe and 9peedy
exit. It Is measurably certain that had
the waste gates been maintained the dam
would never have given way. They were
removed, it is said, because whenever they
were opened the game fish with which the
lake was being stocked would escape. The
fish have escaped all the same, and the lives

A GIGANTIC HEAP OF EARTH.
As to the dam itself, no description yet
printed gives any hint as to Its character.
There was no massive masonry, nor any
tremendous exhibition of engineering skill in
designing the structure or putting it up.
There was no masonry at all in fact, nor
engineering worthy of the name. The dam
i was simply a gigantic heap of earth dumped
1 across the course of a mountain stream
be1 tween two low bills. It was faced on each
i side with a layer of heavy rough stone,
loosely thrown together and uncemented.

) This pile of earth was, as has been stated,
about 75 feet high and 90 feet thick at the
base. At the summit it was levelled off so
i as to be about 20 feet wide, and a wagon
l road crossed it. It was an ordinary dlrt road,
s and there was no rock or masonry beneath
) It The width of the stream

feet long. It was built straight across the
fap, and neither face nor back was curved.
'he slopes were about the same on both
face and back.
Whatever may have been the iudlrec
